background.definition: Infection with the intestinal protozoan parasite, Entamoeba (E.) histolytica, also called amebiasis. Clinically apparent infections may cause diarrhea (colitis), liver abscess, pneumonia, pericarditis, or encephalitis. In the United States, the disease is most often seen in people who have traveled to or are immigrants from tropical places with poor sanitary conditions, people who live in institutions with poor sanitary conditions, and among men who have sex with men.

list.listitem: 1.14 cases per 100,000 in the United States in 1994. The case rate is likely higher in recent years.
The annual incidence rate of amebiasis in Ontario, Canada was 5.1 to 6.4 cases per 100,000 populations, based on data from 2005-2014.
Endemic in developing nations in tropical latitudes (India, Africa, and Central and South America, particularly Mexico).
For global geographic distribution and prevalence of E. histolytica refer to
In 2007, the California Department of Public Health reported 411 cases of amoebiasis and estimated the prevalence of E. histolytica infection in the United States at approximately 4%.

In a study of 55 stool samples from a rural impoverished area of Alabama exposed to open-sewage systems, 19 tested positive for N. americanus (hookworm), four tested positive Stronglyloides stercoralis, and one tested positive for E. histolytica.
The seroprevalence of E. histolytica in some rural communities in Mexico remains as high as 42%.
E. histolytica was detected using PCR in 13.7% of fecal samples in northeast states of India.
E. histolytica seropositivity was found to be 11% among 7 providences in China and was as high as 41% among men having sex with men (MSM) in Beijing and Tianjin.

In a Japanese study of patients with HIV, anti-E. histolytica seroprevalence was 21.3% (277/1303). Eighteen patients (1.5%) among those not previously treated with nitroimidazole developed invasive amebiasis during the treatment-free period; risk was higher in those with a higher titer.

Among 9803 pregnant women in Ethiopia, intestinal parasites were identified in 29% and E. histolytica/dispar in 6% (95% CI 4-8%). A similar rate of infection with E. histolytica/ dispar of 9% (95% CI 3-19%) was found in a global prevalence study of pregnant women.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 46 cross-sectional studies including 29,968 African school children found a pooled prevalence of intestinal protozoan parasites of 25.8% (95% CI: 21.2%-30.3%) with E. histolytica/ dispar identified in 13.3% (95% CI: 10.9%-15.9%).
Approximately 500 million people are infected by E. histolytica worldwide, which is about 10% of the world's population, mostly in developing countries.
Common cause of parasitic death throughout the world, with over 100,000 deaths per year
In the large Global Enteric Multi-Center Study (GEMS), E. histolytica was 1 of the top 10 causative agents of moderate to severe diarrhea in children under the age of five years.

Between the years 1990 and 2007, 134 amebic-related deaths were reported in the US based on death-certificate data. Most deaths occurred in US-born individuals (67.2%) and among residents of California and Texas (58.4%). Rates of amoebiasis-related deaths were the highest in males, Hispanics, Asian/Pacific islanders, and persons 75 years of age and older.
The protozoan Entamoeba histolytica, a single-cell parasite.
Entamoeba dispar is morphologically identical by stool microscopy, but it does not cause symptomatic disease.
Most cases are from ingestion of fecally-contaminated water or food, but exposure to contaminated fecal matter may occur during sexual contact as well.
Ingested cysts hatch into trophozoites in the small intestine.

Symptomatic disease occurs when the trophozoite form of E. histolytica invades the intestinal mucosa. Many patients in tropical areas are chronically infected with E. dispar, which does not invade the intestinal mucosa and is microscopically similar to E. histolytica.

E. histolytica is the only entamoeba species that can modulate the host microbiota, which appears to contribute to symptomatic disease. In addition, secretory IGA plays an important role in resistance to colonization and intestinal invasion.
Trophozoites may enter the blood stream through the portal venous system and travel to the liver, lung, peritoneum, or brain.
In the liver, trophozoites kill hepatocytes which creates the classic appearance of "anchovy paste" chocolate-colored fluid upon drainage.
Several differentially expressed genes have been identified among those with amebiasis compared to healthy controls that may serve as future targets for identification and treatment.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Poor sanitation, low socioeconomic status in developing areas
Recent immigrant from endemic area (esp. South Asia, Middle East, and South America)
Visiting family or doing volunteer/ mission work in an endemic area
Men who have sex with men, living in an endemic area

list.listitem: Consider screening recent immigrants or those who have recently traveled to endemic areas. B
When visiting endemic areas, use proper water purification techniques. C
Drink bottled water and use bottled water for brushing teeth. C
Avoid ice in drinks or foods that may be contaminated (uncooked or unwashed). C
Avoid fresh fruit or vegetables that are not self-peeled; milk, cheese, or dairy products that have not been pasteurized; and food or drinks sold by street vendors. C
Vaccines are under investigation in rodent and nonhuman primate models and appear promising.
Stool microscopy is unable to distinguish between E. histolytica and E. dispar (nonpathogenic). C
Detection of E. histolytica antigens in stool is more sensitive and specific than microscopy, but may not be available in resource limited settings. B
Stool PCR is extremely sensitive and is considered the gold standard for diagnosing amebiasis, although the expense and technical nature of the test can limit its use. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Bloody diarrhea, related to poorly cooked hamburger
Fever, systemic illness, blood or mucous in stools
Diarrhea persisting for more than 2 weeks, usually related to contaminated water
Watery diarrhea with nausea and vomiting, worse in immunocompromised patients
More chronic in nature, no response to antibiotic treatment
More acute in onset; more nausea and vomiting

list.listitem: Most infections (80%-90%) are asymptomatic.
When E. histolytica invades the intestinal mucosa the patient will develop symptoms of colitis, usually 2 to 4 weeks after the initial infection.
Symptoms can include bloody diarrhea, severe abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue, and fever. See

In patients presenting to Canadian travel clinic after immigration or recent international travel, 41/3528 (1.2%) had amebiasis. GI symptoms were the presenting complaint in 32/41 and 1622 of all patients had GI symptoms (sensitivity 78% and specificity 54%).
The pericardium can be involved in cases of E. histolytica amebiasis, resulting in pericardial effusion, acute pericarditis, and potentially cardiac tamponade or constrictive pericarditis.

Important history includes recent travel to a high-risk area (e.g., Indian subcontinent, parts of Central and South America, and parts of Africa), immigration from an endemic area, or family member with amebiasis (see ).
Stool antigen testing for E. histolytica is more sensitive (90.3% vs. 87.1%) and specific (97.7%) than microscopy .

Stool microscopy requires 3 or more specimens, as cysts are shed intermittently; also microscopy can't be used to distinguish between E. histolytica and E. dispar as they are morphologically indistinguishable. A study in a low resource setting (Western Kenya) concluded that compared with PCR microscopy was 64% sensitive and 87% specific (LR+ 4.9, LR- 0.41) for detection of entameba histolytica.

PCR from stool is highly accurate and is endorsed by the World Health Organization, but may not be feasible in resource-limited settings where amebiasis is common. Multiplex molecular assays using PCR technology enable simultaneous detection and identification of multiple pathogens. Authors of meta-analysis of 14 studies using FilmArray GI panel found successful identification of pathogens in 39.7% of patients suffering from gastroenteritis, including 0.3% infected with E. histolytica.

Serology can be helpful with extraintestinal infections (94% sensitive, 95% specific), as stool studies can be negative. Antibodies remain detectable for years after treatment, so only negative serology is helpful for ruling out disease.
A recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) method was used in one study to detect E. histolytica, which was inexpensive and had high sensitivity and specificity.

Colonoscopy with biopsy can also be used to diagnose amebic colitis. In a case series and systematic review of 25 studies, investigators reported primarily finding the characteristically flask-shaped ulcers in the cecum and rectum, an ulcerated mass, and edematous mucosa; biopsy and microscopy was used to confirm Entamoeba species.
No relevant clinical decision rules found.

Asymptomatic patients should be treated with an intraluminal agent such as iodoquinol or paromomycin to destroy cysts. C
Tinidazole may be more effective than metronidazole in treating symptomatic infections, and has fewer side effects. B
Patients with liver abscess do not necessarily need percutaneous drainage. A
Inflammatory bowel disease needs to be ruled out, as treatment with corticosteroids in a patient with amebic colitis can lead to toxic megacolon. B

Asymptomatic patients should be treated with intraluminal amebecide such as iodoquinol (650 mg orally, divided three times daily X 20 days) or paromomycin (25-35 mg/kg total daily oral dose, divided three times daily × 7 days).

For intestinal disease that is symptomatic, treat with metronidazole (750 mg orally three times daily ×10 days) or tinidazole (2 grams orally daily × 3-5 days) AND an intraluminal amebecide (iodoquinol or paromomycin, most commonly).
Nearly all (95%) patients treated with tinidazole demonstrated a negative stool sample. Most (88%) patients treated with metronidazole also demonstrated a negative stool sample at 1 month.

Authors of a Cochrane review found tinidazole to be more effective than metronidazole for reducing clinical failure (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.51; 477 participants, eight trials) based on low-certainty evidence, and is probably associated with fewer adverse events (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.92; 477 participants, 8 trials; moderate-certainty evidence).

In a recent RCT in India including 150 patients hospitalized with amebic liver abscess, more patients randomized to tinidazole compared to metronidazole had an earlier clinical response (within 72 hours; 62.3% vs. 37.7%) and experienced fewer side effects. Similarly, a Cochrane review of 8 RCTs with 477 patients concluded that tinidazole was more effective than metronidazole at reducing clinical failure (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.15-0.51) and appears to be better tolerated as well.
Treament of patients with liver abscess should include metronidazole for 10 days OR tinidazole for 5 days (with close attention to response to therapy) AND an intraluminal amebecide.

In an RCT including 60 patients with uncomplicated amebic liver abscess, clinical response rates were similar for those randomized to metronidazole vs. nitazoxanide, a broad-spectrum antiparasitic and antiviral medication (80% vs. 76.7%, respectively) as were percentages of patients with complete resolution (60% vs. 73.3%, respectively). Although time to achieve symptomatic clinical response was significantly less in the metronidazole group, metronidazole was associated with significantly greater frequency of adverse effects compared to nitazoxanide.

The development of toxic megacolon has been linked to corticosteroid administration before amebic colitis is diagnosed and reduces responsiveness to antiamoebic therapy, sometimes requiring immediate surgical intervention. It is important to exclude amebiasis in high-risk patients before treating inflammatory bowel disease, using the most sensitive and specific test available.
A comparison of drainage to no drainage of amebic liver abscess found no significant difference in response to therapy. A
Percutaneous aspiration and drainage of liver abscess may be helpful if patient is not responding to therapy by about 72 hours or in those at high risk for impending abscess rupture. C
Authors of a meta-analyses of 3 studies found Lepidium virginicum L. effective against E. histolytica.
Hospitalization should be considered if a patient shows signs of dehydration or of possible extraintestinal disease (e.g., liver or lung abscess, pericarditis).
Most patients infected with E. histolytica remain asymptomatic. B
Approximately 10% of patients infected with E. histolytica will develop colitis within 1 year. B
On average more than 50% of patients with severe amebic colitis die. B Among patients with necrotizing colitis, 40% die and those with concomitant liver abscess have a mortality rate of 89%.

Treatment of children with amebic colitis is with the same medications as in adults but in lower doses: Paromomycin 25 to 35 mg/kg/day orally, divided three times daily for 5 to 10 days. Metronidazole 30 to 50 mg/kg/day, divided three times daily for 5 to 10 days. Tinidazole 50 mg/kg/day orally, once daily for 3 days.

In a prospective study of infants born in an urban slum of Dhaka, Bangladesh, 80% of children were infected with E. histolytica by the age of 2 years. In this study there was evidence in support of breastfeeding to improve active and passive immunity. Infants with mothers with high levels of breast milk anti-galactose/ N-acetylgalactosamine lectinimmunoglobulin A had fewer E. histolytica infections, and reinfection was lower in children who had fecal anti-galactose/N-acetylgalactosamine lectin immunoglobulin A, transmitted via maternal breastmilk.
